title: Hasdai ibn Shaprut
hookLine: a Jewish physician and courtier in Córdoba who supported scholars

cards: A study house in Córdoba. The teacher asks a hard question about the law, and nobody can answer. Then a stranger by the door, in ragged clothes, raises his hand and answers it perfectly.

Tradition says he was a scholar captured at sea and ransomed, and before the day was out the community wanted him as their teacher. Making that happen took money, standing, and someone close to the ruler.
In Córdoba, that someone was a Jewish doctor at the caliph's court. Today, Hasdai ibn Shaprut, and what a person does with a seat near power.

teach.h: A DOCTOR WHO OPENS THE PALACE DOOR.
teach.b: Hasdai was a physician, and that opened the palace door.
He served the caliph Abd al-Rahman the Third as a doctor, then as a diplomat and an official who handled foreign envoys and trade: a Jew in the inner circle of a Muslim ruler.
Among Jews he was a leader and protector, the person you went to when a community anywhere was in trouble. What did he do with that place? Three things stand out.
First, the scholar by the door.
The medieval chronicler Abraham ibn Daud tells how the ransomed sage, Moses ben Hanoch, was set up as head of learning in Córdoba, with Hasdai supporting his school.
For a long time Jews in Spain had sent their hardest questions east, to the academies of Babylon. Now they could ask at home.

Second, he paid for poets and grammarians. Two of them, Menahem ben Saruq and Dunash ben Labrat, got into a fierce argument about how Hebrew works, and the argument itself helped grow a new Hebrew poetry in Spain.
Third, a letter attributed to Hasdai reaches out to a faraway king of the Khazars, who was said to rule a Jewish kingdom. An old line from the book of Esther fits him.

teach.h: FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.
teach.b: Mordecai tells Queen Esther, who also had a place near a throne, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?"
A seat near power is not only an honor. In this story it is a job.

how: Jewish tradition honors those who use wealth or influence to support Torah study and protect others, and Jewish communities still raise support for schools, scholars and people in need.

games.why: Abraham ibn Daud's chronicle says the ransomed sage became head of learning in Córdoba with Hasdai's support, so Spanish Jews could ask their questions at home.

practice: You may not sit near a king, but you have some place: a job, a group chat, a skill, a person who listens to you.
Name one, and ask quietly who is outside that door who could use what you can reach: a student, a new neighbor, someone looking for work. If you pray, you can hold that person in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Hasdai. A Jewish physician and official at the court of Córdoba who used his place to support scholars, poets and communities. Today's word.
